params.question: According to Asian-Indian consensus cut-offs, a patient with a BMI of 26 kg/m² is classified as:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: By Western criteria BMI 26 appears near-normal, but South Asians carry significantly more visceral fat at any given BMI. Indian thresholds are set lower to capture this risk.
Asian-Indian overweight begins at BMI 23, but BMI 26 exceeds the Indian obesity threshold of 25 kg/m². This patient has crossed into the obese category.
Correct. Asian-Indian consensus defines obesity as BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² because South Asians develop metabolically dangerous visceral fat at lower body weights than Western populations.
Morbid obesity requires a substantially higher BMI (typically ≥ 37.5 by Indian standards). A BMI of 26 crosses the Indian obesity cut-off of 25 but is not in the morbid range.

overallFeedback.feedback: By Western criteria BMI 26 appears only mildly overweight. However, South Asians carry more visceral fat at the same BMI, so Indian consensus sets the obesity threshold at 25 kg/m², making BMI 26 frank obesity.
Exactly right. South Asians accumulate more visceral fat at any given BMI, which is why Indian obesity begins at 25 kg/m² — five points lower than the Western cut-off of 30.

interactions.label: According to the International Diabetes Federation criteria for metabolic syndro

params.question: According to the International Diabetes Federation criteria for metabolic syndrome, which of the following is the MANDATORY starting criterion?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Elevated fasting glucose is one of the four additional criteria. Any two of four must be present alongside the mandatory starting criterion of central obesity.

answers.text: Central obesity defined by population-specific waist circumference thresholds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The IDF requires central obesity as the mandatory starting point — waist ≥ 90 cm in Indian men, ≥ 80 cm in Indian women — plus any two of four additional criteria (triglycerides, HDL, BP, glucose).
Raised triglycerides are one of the four additional criteria, not the mandatory starting component of the IDF framework.
Raised blood pressure is one of the four additional criteria. The IDF framework places central obesity — not any single metabolic marker — as the required entry point.

overallFeedback.feedback: The IDF criteria require central obesity as the mandatory starting criterion, using population-specific waist cut-offs (≥ 90 cm for Indian men, ≥ 80 cm for Indian women). Then any two of four additional features — triglycerides, HDL, BP, or fasting glucose — complete the diagnosis.
Well done. The IDF framework begins with central obesity because visceral adipose inflammation drives the insulin resistance that connects all other components of the syndrome.

interactions.label: A 42-year-old woman with BMI 35 and irregular menstrual cycles presents for obes

params.question: A 42-year-old woman with BMI 35 and irregular menstrual cycles presents for obesity evaluation. Which of the following history domains is MOST important to explore first, given her presenting features?

answers.text: Twenty-four-hour dietary recall to quantify caloric intake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dietary history is essential in every obesity evaluation, but this patient's irregular menstrual cycles point toward a secondary cause that must be screened for before attributing the obesity to lifestyle alone.

answers.text: Physical activity assessment using a structured questionnaire

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Physical activity is a standard domain, but the combination of obesity with menstrual irregularity suggests a secondary aetiology that should take clinical priority in the history.

answers.text: Screening for secondary causes including polycystic ovary syndrome

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Irregular periods in a woman with obesity should prompt targeted screening for PCOS — one of the key secondary causes. Hypothyroidism and Cushing syndrome must also be considered.
Assessing motivational readiness is important but comes after identifying potential secondary causes. A treatable secondary cause changes the entire management plan.

overallFeedback.feedback: Although all seven domains of the obesity history are important, this patient's irregular menstrual cycles with obesity strongly suggest a secondary cause. Always screen for PCOS, hypothyroidism, and Cushing syndrome before attributing weight gain to lifestyle alone — missing a treatable cause is a serious clinical error.

Exactly. While all seven history domains matter, clinical features like irregular menstrual cycles in the setting of obesity should trigger targeted screening for secondary causes — particularly PCOS — before labelling the condition as primary lifestyle obesity.

interactions.label: Using the Five As framework for obesity counselling, what is the recommended FIR

params.question: Using the Five As framework for obesity counselling, what is the recommended FIRST step when addressing weight with a patient?

answers.text: Assess their current dietary habits and physical activity level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Assessment is the second step in the framework. Before exploring habits, you must first ask the patient's permission to discuss weight — this respects autonomy and builds trust.

answers.text: Advise them on evidence-based caloric reduction targets

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Advising comes third in the Five As. Jumping to prescriptive advice without seeking permission or assessing readiness can damage the therapeutic relationship and increase weight stigma.

Correct. The first A is 'Ask' — requesting permission before discussing weight. This approach respects patient autonomy and reduces weight stigma, which otherwise drives patients away from seeking care.

answers.text: Agree on a shared target of 5–10% weight loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Agreeing on goals comes fourth in the framework. Setting targets before asking permission and assessing readiness can feel prescriptive and undermine patient engagement.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Five As framework starts with 'Ask' — asking permission before discussing weight. This is crucial because weight stigma drives delayed care and compensatory eating. The full sequence is: Ask permission, Assess readiness, Advise using person-first language, Agree on shared goals, Assist with concrete follow-up.

Well done. The Five As — Ask, Assess, Advise, Agree, Assist — begin with seeking permission, reflecting the evidence that patients who feel shamed about their weight are less likely to return for follow-up.

interactions.label: A patient with BMI 29 and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes fails to achieve targe

params.question: A patient with BMI 29 and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes fails to achieve target weight loss after 6 months of structured lifestyle modification. Which pharmacotherapy class offers the HIGHEST weight loss efficacy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Orlistat blocks fat absorption and produces moderate weight loss but causes significant gastrointestinal side effects. It is less effective than GLP-1 receptor agonists.
This combination targets reward and craving pathways and achieves meaningful weight loss, but it does not match the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Correct. GLP-1 RAs, particularly semaglutide, are the most effective pharmacotherapy class for obesity, achieving up to 15% weight loss. They are adjuncts to lifestyle modification, never replacements.
Metformin is primarily an antidiabetic agent with modest weight effects. It is not classified among the main pharmacotherapy options for obesity management discussed in current guidelines.

overallFeedback.feedback: GLP-1 receptor agonists — liraglutide and semaglutide — are the most effective pharmacotherapy class, with semaglutide achieving up to 15% weight loss. Pharmacotherapy is indicated at BMI ≥ 27.5 with a comorbidity, or ≥ 32.5 without, by Indian standards. All agents are adjuncts to lifestyle modification.

Well done. GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide lead the pharmacotherapy ladder with up to 15% weight loss, followed by naltrexone–bupropion and orlistat. All are adjuncts to ongoing lifestyle modification, never stand-alone treatments.
